special_features: Continuous prose with three internal sub-headings ('A Sentimental Journey', 'The Rhetoric of Emotion', 'Discomfort with the Humanities', 'Chapter Outlines'). Sub-headings are inline and not numbered.
Opens with cognitive-science dinner-party scenario (Wilson-Mendenhall et al. 2011, Barsalou lab) — book's first footnote
Closes with chapter-forecasting paragraphs that signpost all four body chapters and the Epilogue
Establishes a seven-mode rhetoric-of-emotion typology (mimetic, cathartic, projective, prosthetic, performative, voluntary, systematic) at PDF pp.20-21 / book pp.10-11
Establishes a four-mode reading of *Imitation of Christ* (mimetic / prosthetic / performative / systematic) at PDF p.24 / book p.14
Berlant Cruel Optimism cited at note 3 (anchor p.5 of Berlant)
Austen Persuasion epigraph: Lady Russell 'must learn to feel that she had been mistaken' (note 2, Oxford ed. p.198)

outline: PDF pp.11-13 (book pp.1-3) — Opening dinner-party scenario from Wilson-Mendenhall et al. 2011 (note 1) establishes that even prototypical situated-emotion stimuli destabilize basic-emotion taxonomies under reread pressure: would the rejected defender feel anger or fear, pride or indignation? Austen's Persuasion (Lady Russell's retroactive emotional revision, note 2) is set against Berlant's situation-comedy/police-procedural definition of *situation* from Cruel Optimism p.5 (note 3) to launch Gross's counter-emphasis on the rhetorically defined *uncomfortable situation*. Sentimental literature, not television, is announced as the optimal research domain. James Chandler's Archaeology of Sympathy (note 5) is engaged, then redirected: rather than an Adam-Smith-to-Capra spectator-archaeology, Gross proposes a 'critical history of well-being' pivoted on eighteenth-century sentimental literature. PDF pp.13-17 (book pp.3-7) — Gross narrates the methodological evolution from his 2006 Secret History of Emotion: the earlier book's polemic against brain science is now repositioned to admit a 'worthwhile science of emotion' once cognitive science itself splits between basic-emotions and situated-emotion paradigms (Griffiths and Scarantino 2009 'Emotions in the Wild' — wedding ceremony, emotional capital, emotional affordances). A thought-experiment about a post-apocalyptic alien learning romantic love by reading Stone, Pinker, and OED is mobilized to argue that narrative literature uniquely models cognitive dynamics ecologically. Reddy's The Making of Romantic Love (note 13) supplies a performative-emotive account ('I love you' as instantiation, not description) and converges with situated-cognitive-science findings that romantic love is not hard-wired. PDF pp.17-19 (book pp.7-9) — Under the 'A Sentimental Journey' sub-heading, Gross reads at length the Yorick-and-the-lady hand-holding passage from Sterne's A Sentimental Journey (1768; note 14): four numbered beats — hand-grasp, English-philosophical reflection, lady's drop-the-hand reply, situation 'regained' — show negation as the operative rhetorical engine of sentiment. Reference to Walter Shandy's 'love is not so much a SENTIMENT as a SITUATION' from Tristram Shandy (note 14) anchors the chapter's coining vocabulary. The passage is then reconnected to Wilson-Mendenhall/Barsalou/Barrett 2011: laboratory studies fail to capture exigence, key-term ordinary-language usage, mediation, and rhetorical interpretation. PDF pp.19-23 (book pp.9-13) — Under 'The Rhetoric of Emotion' Gross replaces the hardwired/constructed binary with a seven-mode typology: 1) mimetic (Ngai's 'literary strategy of sympathy', mirror-neurons, infant-distress kin alignment); 2) cathartic (Aristotle Poetics, Oedipus); 3) projective (Ngai; Lipps's Einfühlung as feeling-into, Mysteries of Udolpho); 4) prosthetic (sublime object; Christ's Passion via 1 Peter 3:14; Susan Miller/Cynthia Haynes 'pathos@play.prosthetic.emotion', note 17); 5) performative (Reddy on 'I love you'); 6) voluntary (Philip Fisher Vehement Passions — Austen's Darcy as 'shamelessly' soliciting reader-shame); 7) systematic (Hobbes's political economy of fear and vainglory; Sterne's Sentimental Journey as self-co-constitutive object-and-theory). The affect/emotion controversy is parsed via Ruth Leys's critique of Brian Massumi (notes 19-21); Raymond Williams's 'creditable emotion' from The Long Revolution (note 23) — the 'feeling of freedom carefully controlled' — is recovered as a rhetorical reference point that neither pure affect-theory nor systematic philosophy (a la Nussbaum) can capture. PDF pp.23-24 (book pp.13-14) — God's love is parsed across the typology: mimetic (Eph 5:2 'walk in love'), prosthetic (John 4:19 'we love Him because He first loved us'), performative ('Jesus loves you'), systematic (Aquinas Summa; Equiano's Mount Calvary 'unseals the book' scene, forecast for ch. 2). PDF pp.24-27 (book pp.14-17) — Under 'Discomfort with the Humanities' Gross critiques the consoling 'cultural scaffolding' / 'jazz ensemble' / 'fabric of each human mind' metaphors of Andy Clark, Hubert Dreyfus, John Haugeland, and Evan Thompson (notes 27-29) as a return-home rhetoric repressing *unheimlich* alienation (Freud, note 30). Uexküll's Umwelt is invoked (note 28); Moretti's The Bourgeois (note 32) supplies *comfort* as a third keyword of bourgeois modernity (Robinson Crusoe 1719 as transition-marker); Sara Ahmed's queer phenomenology of comfort (note 33) and Kurt Lewin's Gestalt 'hopeless situation' plus Wittgenstein's 1938 Lectures on Aesthetics 'discomfort' (note 34) supply the dissensus this book extends. PDF pp.27-37 (book pp.17-27) — Under 'Chapter Outlines' Gross forecasts every chapter: Ch.1 (Darwin disentangled from Ekman; rhetorical reading of Expression of the Emotions; Alva Noë's Out of Our Heads); Ch.2 (Equiano's 'happily situated' as a slave; Du Bois double consciousness; Afro-pessimism via Moten and Sexton; Saidiya Hartman's 'barbarous archive'); a three-dimensional definition of rhetorical theory (effectiveness, transactional pathos, field-guide of threat/promise) keyed to Burke's 'literature as equipment for living' (note 38) and Bitzer's 1968 'rhetorical situation' (note 36) with a one-sentence allusion to Heidegger's 1924 Aristotle lectures on lack-of-composure (Aus-der-Fassung, note 37); Ch.3 (Radcliffe's Romance of the Forest; J.J. Gibson's affordance theory adjusted by abandoning the invariance criterion; Lewis's The Monk and Walpole's Otranto preface; ecocriticism distinguished from literary Darwinism; Antonia's 'undone' and Adeline's affecting nonreferring terms, note 39); Ch.4 (Sense and Sensibility; mixed feelings as negotiated, not Galenic-humoural; Kahneman and Miller 1986 'Norm Theory', note 41; critique of Lisa Zunshine's mind-reading Cognitive-Approaches reading); Epilogue with Stephanie Preston on the persistence of unconscious white/black bias in laboratory fear-studies that defer the causal explanation of racial slavery (note 42, expanded from the Biess/Gross 2014 Science and Emotion after 1945 chapter).

concepts.name: uncomfortable situation
concepts.definition: Titular load-bearing category: a situation defined by rhetorical instability that exposes the constructive layer of emotion, in contrast to Berlant's situation-as-noteworthy-unfolding.

concepts.name: situated conceptualization
concepts.definition: Barsalou-lab cognitive-science paradigm (Wilson-Mendenhall et al. 2011) in which emotion concepts are instantiated in context-dependent, audience-inflected scenarios rather than retrieved from amodal taxonomies.

concepts.name: rhetoric of emotion
concepts.definition: Gross's methodological name for treating emotion as transactional and audience-oriented; 'asserting relationships' in addition to describing them; replaces the hardwired/constructed binary.

concepts.name: mimetic emotion
concepts.definition: Mode 1 of the typology: 'literary strategy of sympathy' (Ngai), tears producing tears; analog in mirror-neuron theory and emotion-recognition; biologically adaptive for kin alignment.

concepts.name: cathartic emotion
concepts.definition: Mode 2: Aristotle's Poetics-style transaction where one emotion (Oedipus' suffering) reliably produces a different specific emotion (pleasant relief) in spectator.

concepts.name: projective emotion
concepts.definition: Mode 3 (after Ngai/Lipps Einfühlung): a subject's appraisal-emotion treated as if it were a property of the work itself (Mysteries of Udolpho is not boring; I am bored).

concepts.name: prosthetic emotion
concepts.definition: Mode 4: the object or scene extends our emotional range; someone suffers in our stead (Passion of Christ, 1 Peter 3:14); rooted in Susan Miller and Cynthia Haynes 'pathos@play.prosthetic.emotion' (note 17).

concepts.name: performative emotion
concepts.definition: Mode 5: 'I love you' (Reddy) instantiates rather than describes the emotion; outcome is uncertain, generic-and-social viability and reception matter materially.

concepts.name: voluntary emotion
concepts.definition: Mode 6 (Philip Fisher Vehement Passions p.142-144): reader supplies the missing affect that the character 'shamelessly' fails to feel — paradigmatic in Austen.

concepts.name: systematic emotion
concepts.definition: Mode 7 (most important for the book): an emotion appears only as part of a system — Hobbesian political economy, or a self-co-constitutive theory like Sterne's Sentimental Journey; allows analysis of emotions that are excluded or unavailable.

concepts.name: four-mode reading of Imitation of Christ
concepts.definition: Worked example at p.14: God's love is simultaneously mimetic (Eph 5:2), prosthetic (John 4:19), performative ('Jesus loves you'), and systematic (Aquinas; Equiano's Mount Calvary 'unseals' the book).

concepts.name: creditable emotion
concepts.definition: Raymond Williams's term (Long Revolution): an emotion that operates as a lived reference point even though it directly contradicts the conditions for its own satisfaction — exemplified by the 'feeling of freedom carefully controlled' in late liberal democracies.

concepts.name: comfort (as bourgeois keyword)
concepts.definition: Following Moretti's The Bourgeois, comfort shifts in the late 17th/early 18th century from a return to normality after adversity to taking normality as starting point and pursuing well-being as an end in itself (Robinson Crusoe 1719 as transitional case).

concepts.name: well-being (critical history of)
concepts.definition: Gross's positive methodological alternative to Chandler's 'archaeology of sympathy': sentimental literature of the eighteenth century is the pivot point at which the terms of our comfort take polemic shape.

concepts.name: rhetorical situation (Bitzer 1968)
concepts.definition: Exigence + audience + constraints (Bitzer Philosophy and Rhetoric 1.1:1-14); 'basic discomfort' is recast by Gross as the operative exigence (note 36).

concepts.name: literature as equipment for living
concepts.definition: Burke's formulation (Philosophy of Literary Form pp.60-61, note 38): poetry is therapeutic/prophylactic equipment against actual or threatened discomfort; recovers the dialectical pair comfort/discomfort against 19th-century decoration-aesthetics.

concepts.name: affordance theory (rhetorical extension)
concepts.definition: J.J. Gibson's ecological-perception affordance is recast by Gross as a humanistic field-guide to threatening/promising environments; the invariance criterion is to be abandoned in ch.3 to capture historically-conditioned hostile environments.

concepts.name: real terror is fictional
concepts.definition: Programmatic claim that terror, unlike a dangerous situation, is the stuff of uncertainties and rhetorical form-of-address; Adeline (Romance of the Forest) demonstrates the affectability of nonreferring terms (after Jami Bartlett, note 39).

concepts.name: mixed feelings (anti-Galenic)
concepts.definition: Sense and Sensibility's titular category: not an internal disequilibrium of humoural components but a socially-negotiated convergence of conflicting alternatives on character; engaged with Kahneman-Miller 'Norm Theory' (1986).

concepts.name: negation (as rhetorical-emotional engine)
concepts.definition: Sterne's signature device by which sentiment appears only through its undoing; semantic and theological negation are jointly load-bearing (forecast to Darwin ch.1).

concepts.name: ambient/situated cognition (critiqued metaphors)
concepts.definition: The 'cultural scaffolding' (Griffiths-Scarantino), 'jazz ensemble' (Clark/Dreyfus), 'covers' / 'embedded' (Haugeland), and 'fabric of each human mind' (Thompson) tropes; read by Gross as a consolatory bourgeois return-home rhetoric.

concepts.name: comfortable philosopher
concepts.definition: Gross's polemical figure for the situated-cognition philosopher who recuperates a comfortable world against unheimlich alienation; the figure is to be unsettled by reading the organizing metaphor against vexed literature.

concepts.name: hostile environment (forecast)
concepts.definition: Forecast for ch.3: the legal-then-literary category that motivates abandoning Gibson's invariance criterion; protected classes (race, color, sex, family status) anchor the legal sense.

concepts.name: bearing up (forecast)
concepts.definition: Forecast for ch.2: Equiano's emotional disposition under slavery — the central question is how Equiano can write he is 'happily situated' as a slave and what this contradiction does to our sciences of emotion.

concepts.name: loss of composure (forecast for ch.1)
concepts.definition: The Darwin-chapter quality of the uncomfortable situation; aligned via note 37 with Heidegger's Aus-der-Fassung from the 1924 Aristotle lectures.

concepts.name: irreconcilable difference (forecast for epilogue)
concepts.definition: Question-marked titular framework for the Preston-coauthored epilogue; classic laboratory fear-studies persistence of unconscious white/black bias requires the situational-rhetorical reframing of racial slavery's causal weight.

concepts.name: affectability of nonreferring terms
concepts.definition: Following Jami Bartlett Object Lessons (2016, note 39): fictional sentences like 'Antonia was raped' or 'X was raped' generate affect through grammatical-semantic possibility rather than reference.

positions.claim: Emotion is neither biologically hardwired nor purely socially constructed; the rhetorical situation determines what we mean by 'emotion' in the first place.
positions.support_evidence: PDF p.19 explicit rejection of 'Emotions: hardwired or socially constructed?' binary as collapsing phenomenology; PDF p.24 four-mode reading of Imitation of Christ.
positions.contested_by: Paul Ekman (basic emotions program); Brian Massumi (autonomy of affect as pre-ideological)

positions.claim: Berlant's situation-as-state-of-things-unfolding (Cruel Optimism p.5) must be supplemented by a rhetorical account of audience investments that defines situations by their emotional instability.
positions.support_evidence: PDF p.12: explicit modification of Berlant's definition; sentimental literature offered as superior research domain to television.
positions.contested_by: Lauren Berlant (in source text only — Gross frames as supplement, not contestation)

positions.claim: Sentimental literature establishes the norms of well-being that the bourgeois eighteenth century inherits and that we still reference; it provides the pivot for a 'critical history of well-being' rather than an 'archaeology of sympathy'.
positions.support_evidence: PDF pp.12-13 redirection of Chandler's An Archaeology of Sympathy (Chandler note 5; Goldsmith note 6).

positions.claim: Affect and emotion should not be valorized one against the other; Raymond Williams's 'creditable emotion' shows how the rhetorical-ideological character of emotion remains analytically essential even after the affective turn.
positions.support_evidence: PDF pp.22-23 close reading of Williams Long Revolution p.321 (note 23); critique of Massumi via Leys (notes 20-21).
positions.contested_by: Brian Massumi; post-Massumi affect theorists who treat affect as pre-ideological/pre-subjective/pre-linguistic

positions.claim: The dominant metaphors of situated cognition theory ('cultural scaffolding', jazz ensemble, fabric of the mind) recuperate bourgeois comfort and repress unheimlich alienation; the queer-Gestalt-Wittgenstein tradition (Lewin, Wittgenstein 1938, Sara Ahmed) supplies an uncomfortable counter-tradition.
positions.support_evidence: PDF pp.25-27, naming Clark, Dreyfus, Haugeland, Thompson; Freud Unbehagen note 30; Ahmed note 33; Lewin/Wittgenstein note 34.
positions.contested_by: Andy Clark; Hubert Dreyfus; John Haugeland; Evan Thompson

positions.claim: Darwin's Expression of the Emotions in Man and Animals is a rhetorical text; Paul Ekman's heavy-handed editorial mediation has done Darwin's science a profound disservice by misreading the photographic illustrations as evidence for universal basic emotions rather than as arguments.
positions.support_evidence: PDF p.28 (book p.18) chapter-1 forecast; alignment with Alva Noë Out of Our Heads (2009).
positions.contested_by: Paul Ekman; advocates of Cognitive Approaches to Literature drawing on Ekman

positions.claim: Mixed feelings are not Galenic disequilibrium but socially-negotiated convergences of conflicting alternatives on character; Austen's Sense and Sensibility critiques the disequilibrium model and pre-figures Kahneman-Miller's 'Norm Theory'.
positions.support_evidence: PDF pp.35-37 (book pp.25-27); Kahneman and Miller 'Norm Theory' Psychological Review 93.2 (1986): 136-153 (note 41).
positions.contested_by: Galenic humoural tradition; Lisa Zunshine (mind-reading Cognitive Approaches reading of Austen)

positions.claim: There is nothing in current neuroscience of sexual desire or romantic love that supports hard-wired-brain-systems orchestration; cultural determinants play a substantial role.
positions.support_evidence: Reddy The Making of Romantic Love p.15, quoted PDF pp.16-17.
positions.contested_by: Hardwired-brain-system models in cognitive neuroscience of emotion

tensions.gross_position: False binary; the rhetorical situation determines what 'emotion' means in the first place.

tensions.tension: Berlant's situation (state of things unfolding) vs. Gross's situation (rhetorical instability)
tensions.gross_position: Audience investments and emotional instability are constitutive of the situation; sentimental literature beats television as research domain.

tensions.tension: Chandler's archaeology of sympathy (spectator) vs. Gross's critical history of well-being (situation)
tensions.gross_position: The sentimental moment in fiction inaugurates the basic situation supposed-to-be-comfortable; we should historicize the terms of our comfort polemically.
Neither term should be valorized over the other; Williams's 'creditable emotion' shows that the ideological-rhetorical character of emotion remains analytically essential.

tensions.tension: Consoling metaphors of situated cognition (cultural scaffolding / jazz / fabric of mind) vs. uncomfortable Gestalt-queer-Wittgenstein counter-tradition
tensions.gross_position: Dominant situated-cognition metaphors are bourgeois return-home rhetoric repressing unheimlich alienation; Lewin, Wittgenstein 1938, Sara Ahmed supply the uncomfortable alternative.
Forecast: Darwin's Expression is rhetorical; the photographic illustrations are arguments; Ekman's editorial reading has done Darwin a disservice.
Forecast: Equiano apparently slips into Kahneman hedonic psychology and Noë/Merleau-Ponty situated cognition but ultimately resists; rhetorical analysis of well-being is the load-bearing tool.

tensions.tension: Galenic disequilibrium mixed-feelings vs. socially-negotiated mixed feelings (Austen)
tensions.gross_position: Mixed feelings are not internal humoural proportions but negotiated convergences of contradictory norms on a focal character.

tensions.tension: Cognitive Approaches mind-reading (Zunshine) vs. Kahneman-Miller norm-theory rhetorical situation
tensions.gross_position: Forecast: theory-of-mind / mind-reading approaches to Austen are unecological; resource distribution and norm-establishment are the actual operative dynamics.

interlocutors.role: Cruel Optimism note 3 anchor; situation-definition that Gross supplements rhetorically; also edited the Darwin essay for Critical Inquiry 37.1 (2010).

interlocutors.name: Jane Austen
interlocutors.role: Persuasion epigraph (Lady Russell); forecast for ch.4 Sense and Sensibility.

interlocutors.name: Laurence Sterne
interlocutors.role: A Sentimental Journey extended set-piece pp.17-19; Tristram Shandy 'love is not so much a SENTIMENT as a SITUATION'.

interlocutors.name: James Chandler
interlocutors.role: An Archaeology of Sympathy — Gross redirects from spectator-archaeology to critical history of well-being.

interlocutors.name: Lawrence Barsalou
interlocutors.role: Senior author of Wilson-Mendenhall et al. 2011; lab whose situated-conceptualization framework grounds Gross's openings.

interlocutors.name: Lisa Feldman Barrett
interlocutors.role: Co-author Wilson-Mendenhall et al. 2011; later cited in ch.4.

interlocutors.name: Paul Ekman
interlocutors.role: Strawman of basic-emotions program; chapter-1 antagonist whose editorial mediation of Darwin is to be peeled away.

interlocutors.name: William M. Reddy
interlocutors.role: Making of Romantic Love supplies the performative-emotive theory ('I love you' instantiates) and the negative result on hardwired-brain neuroscience.

interlocutors.name: Hubert Dreyfus
interlocutors.role: Situated-cognition metaphor critic (jazz ensemble fluid-coping); but also leap-of-existence ally via Kierkegaard (note 31).

interlocutors.name: Andy Clark
interlocutors.role: Supersizing the Mind — dance/jazz metaphor critiqued; David Chalmers's foreword cited (note 27).

interlocutors.name: John Haugeland
interlocutors.role: 'Intimately embedded' / 'covers' metaphor critiqued.

interlocutors.name: Evan Thompson
interlocutors.role: Mind in Life — 'fabric of each human mind' metaphor critiqued.

interlocutors.name: Jakob von Uexküll
interlocutors.role: Foray into the Worlds of Animals and Humans p.172 — sets the stage for environment-organism metaphor system (note 28).

interlocutors.name: Sigmund Freud
interlocutors.role: Psychoanalytic ambivalence as neighbor-position; Civilization and Its Discontents (Das Unbehagen in der Kultur) note 30 anchor for unheimlich.

interlocutors.name: Erving Goffman
interlocutors.role: Sociological uneasiness — named neighbor of Gross's project (no extended treatment).

interlocutors.name: Martin Heidegger
interlocutors.role: Verstimmung as bad-mood neighbor (p.2); note 37 invokes the 1924 Aristotle lectures (GA 18, Michalski ed. p.261) on Aus-der-Fassung — bridge to BCAP heritage.

interlocutors.name: Adam Smith
interlocutors.role: Sympathy as 'feeling what we ourselves should feel in a like situation' (via Chandler p.302); ironized in the Sterne Yorick scene.

interlocutors.name: Brian Massumi
interlocutors.role: 'Autonomy of Affect' Cultural Critique 31 (1995); Parables for the Virtual; Gross uses Leys's critique to qualify Massumi's pre-ideological affect.

interlocutors.name: Ruth Leys
interlocutors.role: 'The Turn to Affect: A Critique' Critical Inquiry 37.3 (2011); structures the affect/emotion controversy.

interlocutors.name: Raymond Williams
interlocutors.role: Long Revolution — 'creditable emotion' and 'feeling of freedom carefully controlled' as historicist rhetorical reference points.

interlocutors.name: Franco Moretti
interlocutors.role: The Bourgeois — comfort as third keyword; Weber Protestant-Ethic Bequemlichkeit; Robinson Crusoe 1719 transition.

interlocutors.name: Sara Ahmed
interlocutors.role: Queer Phenomenology — comfort, disorientation, alienation; concealed domestic labor (Husserl's wife).

interlocutors.name: J. J. Gibson
interlocutors.role: Affordance theory; foundational for ch.3 ecocriticism of the rhetorical sort; Thomas Reid background (note 15).

interlocutors.name: Kenneth Burke
interlocutors.role: Philosophy of Literary Form — comfort/discomfort dialectic; literature as equipment for living; sentimental literature as consolatio philosophiae.
